title: Your first minute in the Hall
promise: Start a concert, choose a piece, and take the music with you.

steps.title: Begin with Satie
steps.text: Start the First Gymnopédie if it is paused. The concert continues from one recording to the next. Space pauses; N and P move between pieces when no control has focus.

steps.title: Watch the written music
steps.text: Choose Score. The gold bar follows this recording; touch a bar to hear it. Automatic alignment is a listening aid, not a claim of note-exact timing.

steps.title: Choose your own programme
steps.text: Open the programme to choose any recording. The concert is ordered by composers’ births; movements of one work stay together.

steps.title: Return to the music
steps.text: Close the programme without stopping the recording. The question-mark button always brings you back to this tour.

steps.title: The music comes with you
steps.text: This bar belongs to the whole site, not one page. Visited pages can be read again offline after caching; streamed recordings still need a connection. Your last recording is remembered, paused, on a return visit.

title: Read a score by listening
promise: Hear the score light up as Satie’s Gymnopédie plays.

steps.title: Let the piano begin
steps.text: Start the First Gymnopédie. This is a recording of Satie’s music, not a recording of Satie himself.

steps.title: Choose Score
steps.text: The engraved page preserves the notation. The moving gold bar follows the performance; the alignment has not yet been checked by ear.

steps.title: Read the qualification
steps.text: The caption identifies the score and the timing method. You can touch a bar on the page to move the recording there.

steps.title: Try Notes
steps.text: The note roll separates the voices by colour. It follows written pitches rather than guessing notes from the sound.

title: Five ways to see the music
promise: Follow Beethoven’s Fifth from score to orchestra, form and sound.
feature: Score · Notes · Orchestra · Form · Sound · F

steps.title: Start Beethoven’s Fifth
steps.text: Start the recording if it is paused. These views share one recording and one position: changing the view never restarts the music.

steps.title: Score: the printed page
steps.text: Choose Score to follow the engraved bars. A gold highlight follows the automatically aligned recording.

steps.title: Notes: separate the voices
steps.text: Choose Notes to see the written pitches as coloured lines. Their lengths follow the score, not measured releases in the recording.

steps.title: Orchestra: who is playing?
steps.text: Choose Orchestra. Instrument groups glow while their parts sound. Boléro also has an orchestra view, with changes placed by passage.

steps.title: Form: hear the returns
steps.text: Choose Form. Sections stretch along the recording; arcs connect returning material. Touch a section to hear its beginning.

steps.title: Sound: the recording itself
steps.text: Choose Sound. The spectrogram measures frequency and loudness in the recording; the heard-harmony estimate is not a transcription.

steps.title: Fill the Hall
steps.text: Press F, or use this corner button, to enlarge the current view. Press F again to return. Escape closes this tour.

steps.title: Keep listening as you read
steps.text: The same player continues here. Open another chapter or lesson without stopping the concert; pause from this bar whenever you want.

title: Hear how a section turns
promise: Hear the silence before Beethoven’s horn call, then inspect the evidence.
feature: As it plays · The joins · ◆ · How we know

steps.title: Open The joins
steps.text: The joins explain how one section becomes another: a silence, a pivot, a change of texture. Each account names what you can hear.

steps.title: Hear the first join
steps.text: Replay the passage around the silence before the horn call. The button begins before the boundary so you hear the preparation.

steps.title: Find the diamonds
steps.text: Each diamond marks a join on the timeline. Select one to hear the surrounding passage rather than only the instant of change.

steps.title: Return to As it plays
steps.text: Live notes follow the recording. The join card appears when the music reaches its boundary.

steps.title: Ask how we know
steps.text: Open this note’s evidence. Score-aligned, measured, documented and general descriptions make different claims about precision.

title: Check a recording’s origins
promise: Check where a recording comes from, what is uncertain, and how to cite it.
feature: This recording · dossiers · other performances · downloads

steps.title: Open This recording
steps.text: The recording tab separates the work from this particular performance, carrier and digital transfer.

steps.title: Read the status of each field
steps.text: Documented means a cited source states it. Inferred means reasoned from evidence. Disputed retains alternatives. An unknown date is left unknown.

steps.title: Find other performances
steps.text: These links open comparisons of the same music. A different transfer or remake is not automatically the same performance.

steps.title: Cite this recording
steps.text: Keep the performer, recording source and Hall link together. A composition’s date is not its recording date.

steps.title: Take the evidence with you
steps.text: Download the recording register as CSV or JSON. Values, evidence statuses, source locators and alternatives remain separate fields.

steps.title: Choose the 1919 reference
steps.text: This Edison performance supplies the shared timeline. Select it before starting; the other cards identify later recordings and their sources.

steps.title: Start the reference
steps.text: Press Play at the listening desk. When you change performer, the comparison maps the current musical position into the other recording.

steps.title: Move into the phrase
steps.text: Move to 42 seconds in the reference, away from the opening lead-in. The map is automatic: matched position does not mean note-exact correspondence.

steps.title: Switch to 1928
steps.text: Choose the electrical Victor remake. Listen for the phrase continuing at its matched position, not at the same number of elapsed seconds.

steps.title: Read the tempo map
steps.text: Above one means the performer takes longer over the corresponding music than the reference. The line describes local time ratios, not absolute tempo markings.

steps.title: Compare a marked passage
steps.text: The passage buttons play the same span through the available performers, then stop. Try one now, or finish the tour and continue switching freely.

title: Follow the Dies irae
promise: Trace the Dies irae from chant to Rachmaninoff.
feature: Influence · thread chips · evidence · deep links

steps.title: One tune, several afterlives
steps.text: The Dies irae chip selects a thread through the web. Portraits are people; the gold connections are specific, sourced relationships.

steps.title: Hear the chant’s outline
steps.text: Play the engraved opening. This is synthesised notation, not a historical recording; the caption explains the editorial rhythm and tempo.

steps.title: Follow it to Rachmaninoff
steps.text: Open the Isle of the Dead connection. Thread stops are dated encounters or works, not a claim that every composer borrowed from the previous stop.

steps.title: Distinguish claim from proof
steps.text: Read the evidence status and its qualification. A familiar melodic outline is not, by itself, proof of a documented encounter.

steps.title: Open the source trail
steps.text: These references support this connection. The address now begins #edge-; a portrait uses #node-, and a complete motif thread uses #thread-. Copy the address to share the same view.

title: Compare an inheritance
promise: Put Vivaldi’s violin line beside Bach’s organ transcription.

steps.title: Source and transformation
steps.text: This connection identifies Vivaldi’s RV 522 and Bach’s BWV 593. The claim concerns a particular transcription, not a general resemblance.

steps.title: Hear the violin line
steps.text: Play the source’s opening two bars. This synthesised example isolates the first violin in the original A minor.

steps.title: Hear the organ line
steps.text: Now play Bach’s uppermost line. The caption states which inner voices have been omitted; open the score source to inspect the fuller texture.

steps.title: Keep the comparison accountable
steps.text: The sources belong to this connection. Follow their locators before using the example as evidence in your own writing.

title: Find a place in time
promise: Find who was in Vienna in 1900, then follow Mahler’s places.
feature: Map · year slider · composer routes · city lists

steps.title: Set the year
steps.text: The Map opens here at 1900. Drag the year slider to change the visible lives; the recorded route is not a reconstruction of every journey.

steps.title: Follow Mahler
steps.text: Mahler is selected. The numbered list records places with dates and sources; the map connects records, not known roads.

steps.title: Listen from a place
steps.text: These buttons use the shared player. A place’s exact work matches are distinguished from other recordings by that composer.

steps.title: Who overlapped in Vienna?
steps.text: Open Encounters for the selected city. Overlapping dates establish a possibility of contact, not proof that the two people met.

steps.title: Read the city’s records
steps.text: Check the dates and sources beside each possible overlap. Use Find a city to compare another place, or Follow a composer to return to a life.

title: Let a story lead the listening
promise: Follow the Vienna 1900 journey through music, paintings and sources.

steps.title: Begin Vienna 1900
steps.text: Begin starts the first excerpt. The stations follow the recordings continuously; pause whenever you want more time with a painting or paragraph.

steps.title: Read beside the music
steps.text: The current station pairs a particular recording with narration and an exhibit. Listening notes change as the excerpt plays.

steps.title: Check this station’s sources
steps.text: Open the recording and source details. The excerpt’s start and end are given beside a link to the complete recording in the Hall.

steps.title: Turn to the next station
steps.text: Use Next, the numbered rail or the arrow keys outside this tour. Your place is saved for a later visit; closing a tour does not stop the music.

title: Read, trace, cite
promise: Find Mahler’s key ideas and sources, then cite a page.
feature: Atlas · composer chapters · inheritance · reading · citation

steps.title: Begin with the key ideas
steps.text: These statements introduce the chapter’s listening vocabulary. Use the chapter contents to move between the life, works, places and sources.

steps.title: Trace what came in
steps.text: Inheritance links lead to specific connections in the Web of Influence. Each connection keeps its own evidence and qualification.

steps.title: Choose a source to read
steps.text: The reading list names books, catalogues and articles. Its notes tell you which question each item helps answer.

steps.title: Copy the Chicago citation
steps.text: Copy the citation, then replace the suggested access date with the date you consulted the page. No publication date is asserted.

steps.title: Or use BibTeX
steps.text: Open the BibTeX entry if your reference manager uses it. The citation identifies this page, not every source quoted within it.

title: Find the word you heard
promise: Hear sonata form, open a definition, and search the whole Atlas.

steps.title: A term beside real music
steps.text: Sonata form is explained here with Beethoven’s Fifth. Definitions link to related terms and recording passages, not only to other definitions.

steps.title: Hear the example
steps.text: Hear it moves the shared player to a particular passage. The caption distinguishes a provisional bar alignment from an editorial listening pointer.

steps.title: Read a definition in place
steps.text: Hover over an underlined term, or reach it with Tab, to open its glossary popover. On a touch screen, tap once. The popover links to the fuller definition.

steps.title: Search from any page
steps.text: Use Search, or press /. On a small screen, Search is inside Menu. Results include composers, works, recordings, ideas and these guide lessons. A lesson result returns to its card here.

title: Hear what changes on return
promise: Compare Beethoven’s exposition with its recapitulation, bar by bar.

steps.title: Hear the first statement
steps.text: A plays the marked exposition passage and stops at its end. The timestamps belong to this recording, not to every performance.

steps.title: Hear its return
steps.text: B plays the corresponding passage in the recapitulation. Listen for what changes when the music returns towards the home key.

steps.title: Read the bar grid
steps.text: Corresponding bars share a column even when they take different lengths of time. Hatched gaps mark bars without a counterpart; colours identify voices.

steps.title: Separate notation from measurement
steps.text: Written differences come from the score. Timings depend on provisional alignment; note lengths are warped notation, not measured releases.
